title: A spin on Hagedorn temperatures and string stars

A spin on Hagedorn temperatures and string stars

Josef Seitza and Erez Y. Urbachb

a Department of Particle Physics and Astrophysics, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot, Israel

b School of Natural Sciences, Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, NJ 08540, USA

josef-emanuel.seitz@weizmann.ac.il

urbach@ias.edu

Abstract

We discuss the correspondence between highly excited strings and black holes in the presence of angular momentum. At fixed imaginary angular velocity , we show that free strings exhibit a Hagedorn instability due to a thermal-winding mode turning tachyonic. This allows us to determine the exact Hagedorn temperature for bosonic, type II, and heterotic strings. Using the effective field theory for the thermal-winding mode around the -dependent background, we find a novel ‘rotating string star’ saddle (perturbatively in the angular velocity) and study its properties. This configuration describes a self-gravitating bound state of highly excited rotating strings. As in the non-rotating case, the saddle is qualitatively shown to interpolate between the rotating strings phase and a rotating black hole. We also comment on the implications of these results for anti-de Sitter space.

1 Introduction

Over time, black holes tend to shrink as they radiate. The fate of small (highly-curved) black holes in a UV-complete theory of gravity is therefore an interesting self-consistency check [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], which could teach us a lesson on black hole microscopy. In string theory, the nature of black holes as their horizon size reaches the string scale remains an open question [8, 9, 10, 11]. One version of this question is phrased in terms of Euclidean gravity [12]. The Euclidean black hole saddle in asymptotically string theory1 is well described by Einstein gravity for , but what is its description for ? Horowitz and Polchinski [15] suggested that at high temperatures and for , the saddle is a normalizable condensate of strings winding on the thermal cycle of . The saddle, interpreted as a self-gravitating stringy condensate [16, 17], is termed ‘the Horowitz-Polchinski solution’ or a ‘string star’. Surprisingly, this saddle carries an thermal entropy, and qualitatively agrees with black hole thermodynamics at lower temperatures.2 Recently, there has been a renewed interest in string stars, extending the original setting [12, 18] to higher dimensions  [19, 20, 21, 22, 23], and other background geometries [14, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30].

To gather more evidence for this proposal, it is natural to consider extra parameters to turn on, both at the string star and the black hole sides of the correspondence. In this work, we study the correspondence in the presence of angular momenta.3 Let be a rotation generator in a two-dimensional plane of . To add angular momenta, we consider an ensemble of fixed temperature , and fixed imaginary ‘angular velocity’ potential , conjugate to , with the partition function

(1.1)

In terms of Euclidean string theory, this ensemble is defined by an asymptotic boundary condition with a twist between the thermal and the angular directions. The twisted is one possible saddle that contributes to , describing, at , freely rotating strings. The Euclidean rotating black hole is another saddle with the same asymptotics that contributes to (1.1). This work suggests a description of the rotating black hole saddle when it reaches a string size . Following the non-rotating case, we find a normalizable winding condensate solution on top of the twisted background. The result is a ‘rotating string star’ saddle, interpreted as a bound state of self-gravitating rotating strings. By studying the saddle thermodynamic properties, we find a qualitative agreement with the rotating black hole (see figure 1).

We begin in section 2 by reviewing the thermodynamic properties of highly-excited rotating strings.4 By studying free strings in the ensemble (1.1), we find it shares an important property with the canonical (non-rotating ) ensemble: it has a Hagedorn instability! Explicitly, we find that due to the high energy spectrum of free rotating strings, diverges at temperatures above a -dependent Hagedorn temperature .5 Defining , we find (for )

We give two alternative ways to find (1.2). One is to directly check the Hagedorn growth of the partition function due to high-energy excitations. A second, more instructive way for our purposes is to follow [42, 43, 13] and interpret the Hagedorn instability as a tachyonic instability of a thermal winding mode in . Studying the winding sector of the twisted worldsheet theory, we were able to derive (1.2). As we explain, it is also possible to derive (1.2) perturbatively in from a target space analysis. Using a Kaluza-Klein (KK) reduction, we find a novel ( dependent) effective field theory (EFT) for the thermal winding mode on . In this way, the Hagedorn temperature (1.2) is the temperature at which a winding mode turns massless.

In section 3, we follow [15] and employ this -dimensional EFT of the winding mode coupled to gravity to find a normalizable winding condensate, or a rotating string star.6 To find the solution, we employ perturbation theory in , which to leading order amounts to a rigid-body approximation. By analytically continuing the solution back to real angular velocity (), we write down the thermodynamic properties of the rotating string star saddle. The rotating string star shares many properties with the non-rotating solution, such as entropy. The winding profile is invariant to the remaining rotation symmetry group and thus has no intrinsic spin. Notably, this solution still carries a non-zero angular momentum, due to the non-trivial dependence, similar to the rotating black hole. In section 4, we compare these properties to rotating black holes and to free strings. As in the non-rotating case, we find qualitative agreement between both in their intermediate parameter regimes.

Finally, in section 5 we follow [14, 24] and discuss the extension of our results to anti-de Sitter (AdS) space. We compute the leading behavior of the AdS Hagedorn temperature in , and comment on the expected properties of the rotating AdS string star.

2.3 A Euclidean derivation of

Following the work of [42, 43, 13], there is a second, intuitive way to explain the Hagedorn instability of string theory in the canonical ensemble. The idea is to follow [57], and understand the canonical partition function as the Euclidean string theory partition function on (with anti-periodic boundary condition for the fermions). In terms of the Euclidean theory, the Hagedorn instability is a divergence of the 1-loop path integral in this background. Unlike field theory, string theory in this background includes sectors of strings winding around the thermal circle. Due to their extension along the thermal circle, the mass of the winding strings is, up to an overall constant, proportional to . A direct computation shows that the lightest winding mode turns massless at the Hagedorn temperature , and tachyonic for higher temperatures. As it becomes massless, the 1-loop partition function acquires a new divergence at , and turns ill-defined for . This is the Euclidean reasoning behind the linear Hagedorn growth of the entropy.

3 The (slowly) rotating string star

In the previous section, we studied properties of free strings. In this section, we turn on the string coupling , or the gravitational constant . Instead of the free string partition function (2.14), we will consider the string theory partition function with only asymptotically geometry (times some compact manifold to saturate the appropriate critical dimension, which we will suppress), twisted by some (2.21). Perturbatively in , we can consider different saddles of the partition function with these boundary conditions. One such saddle is the twisted itself, representing weakly-interacting thermal strings in flat space. Another is the (rotating) Euclidean black hole saddle, in which the thermal circle shrinks with an topology. This saddle remains under control (weakly-curved) only for . 4 The correspondence principle

The main importance of the string star saddle was the suggestion by Horowitz and Polchinski [15] that it interpolates between the black hole and the free string phases of string theory. More precisely [12], the suggestion is that as a Euclidean saddle defined close to , it is continuously connected to the Euclidean black hole at lower temperatures . In other words, as the Euclidean black hole size reaches the string scale, its Einstein gravity description is no longer valid, and should now be described as a self-gravitating string. In this context, this is what is usually referred to as the correspondence principle, or the black hole-string transition. The main argument in favor of this suggestion was that extrapolating the thermodynamic properties of both saddles to an intermediate regime (where both are ill defined), gives qualitatively the same result.

In the other direction, close enough to the Hagedorn temperature, the string star amplitude goes to zero, and we expect it to reduce to the free string phase of the thermal background. This is better described in terms of the microcanonical ensemble. The free string phase is expected to dominate the ensemble at low energies. For high enough energies, the free string self-gravitation can no longer be ignored, and we expect a transition to the string star description. Here as well, a simple extrapolation qualitatively gives the same answer.

In the previous section, we derived the properties of the rotating string star saddle to leading non-trivial order in the angular velocity (or in the microcanonical ensemble). In this section, we discuss the extension of the correspondence arguments to the rotating string star saddle, at leading order in . This requires a comparison to rotating black holes on one side and rotating free strings on the other. As we will see, the qualitative arguments seem to hold in a similar manner also for the (slowly) rotating case.
